question: When object-property combinations are held out in visually rich synthetic VQA worlds, do dataset-trained slot representations support stronger compositional generalization than dense DINOv2 or SigLIP2 features after varying downstream capacity, representation size, training diversity, sample count, and downstream compute?

key_findings.claim: The paper contributes a large controlled VQA testbed spanning three multi-object renderers, three nominal composition difficulties, and a fixed held-out combination set.
key_findings.evidence: For CLEVRTex, Super-CLEVR, and MOVi-C, each nominal training set contains 48,000 images split 40k/4k/4k for train/validation/ID test, plus a 4,000-image COOD test. Roughly 42 question–answer pairs per image yield about 1.7M training and 170k test pairs. CLEVRTex and MOVi-C use 80/40/20% of object combinations for easy/medium/hard training; Super-CLEVR is reduced to 10/5/1% because larger fractions behave nearly in-distribution.

key_findings.claim: The hard MOVi-C split cannot satisfy the stated definition of compositional generalization as recombining only individually seen properties.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says every COOD object combines properties individually observed in training. Appendix A defines MOVi-C objects as 36 shapes × 3 sizes = 108 combinations and hard training as 20%, or only about 22 allowed combinations. Even if every allowed combination used a different shape, at least 14 of the 36 shape values would be absent; some test cases must therefore require unseen-property/category generalization, not only unseen recombination. Super-CLEVR hard uses about 27 random combinations for 21 shapes and supplies no stratified coverage guarantee either.

anchors.section: A Data Generation and split proportions

key_findings.claim: The evaluated object-centric representations are compact, dataset-trained Slot Attention bottlenecks on top of dense foundation features rather than off-the-shelf alternatives with matched training histories.
key_findings.evidence: DINOv2 emits 256×384 patch features and SigLIP2 emits 196×768; DINOSAURv2 and the new SigLIPSAUR2 emit seven 256-dimensional slots. The authors pretrain a separate object-centric model for every dataset variant to reconstruct the dense features, using 300k steps, whereas the original dense encoders receive no analogous dataset-specific representation adaptation.

key_findings.claim: Because object-centric models alone receive 300k steps of in-domain pretraining, the experiments do not isolate object-centric representation structure from dataset adaptation and extra optimization.
key_findings.evidence: The paper describes its comparison as isolating representation structure, and adds jointly trained downstream cross-attention as a size-control for dense features. But Slot Attention is pretrained per easy/medium/hard dataset variant on the target images, while the dense baseline and its resizing layer are not given a matched feature-reconstruction or adaptation phase. Better inductive bias, compression, in-domain adaptation, and training budget therefore remain bundled.

key_findings.claim: With the smaller two-layer downstream transformer, slot representations usually improve COOD accuracy, especially on CLEVRTex and under lower training diversity.
key_findings.evidence: Relative to DINOv2, DINOSAURv2 changes TF2 COOD by +7.0/+12.3/+5.6 points on CLEVRTex, −0.3/+1.6/+1.2 on Super-CLEVR, and +1.0/+1.1/+1.6 on MOVi-C across easy/medium/hard. SigLIPSAUR2 improves on SigLIP2 in all nine TF2 cells by +1.5 to +9.7 points. Seven-token k-means and cross-attention compression generally underperform the pretrained slot bottleneck.

key_findings.claim: With the larger five-layer downstream model, the headline object-centric advantage becomes conditional and the hardest-setting differences are mostly sub-point ties.
key_findings.evidence: Dense encoders often win easy and medium settings. For hard splits, DINOSAURv2 differs from DINOv2 by +0.1, +0.4, and 0.0 points across the three worlds; SigLIPSAUR2 differs from SigLIP2 by +0.9, −0.8, and +0.7. Without repeated-run dispersion, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, these small gaps cannot establish consistent superiority.

key_findings.claim: Slot representations offer a favorable downstream-Transformer FLOP trade-off, but the paper's 'compute efficiency' is not an end-to-end compute comparison.
key_findings.evidence: On Super-CLEVR with DINO-family features, DINOSAURv2 dominates at small downstream budgets; on easy, dense DINOv2 needs about 1.5× downstream compute to match and 3× to gain 3.5 points, while on hard it does not catch up within 3×. The accounting explicitly ignores cross-attention resizing FLOPs and excludes vision-feature extraction and the slot models' 300k-step pretraining. It also allocates more optimization steps to smaller representations under an equal downstream-FLOP budget.

key_findings.claim: The sample-size sweep supports a practical low-data advantage for slots, while also showing that combination diversity matters more than raw image count.
key_findings.evidence: Training subsets range from 2^10 to 2^15 images plus the full 40k. On MOVi-C easy, OC features lead across sizes with TF2; dense features catch or slightly surpass only at the largest diverse sample with TF5. Across worlds, about 2^14 images from easy often match or beat a full medium dataset. The curves are informative but show no multiple split draws, seeds, or uncertainty.

anchors.section: Figures 4–5 and Sample Size vs Diversity

key_findings.claim: Ground-truth object properties do not solve hard COOD, revealing that the learned VQA reasoner and dataset protocol—not only the visual representation—are major generalization bottlenecks.
key_findings.evidence: The oracle reaches near-perfect ID with TF5, but hard COOD is only 76.2% on CLEVRTex, 67.0% on Super-CLEVR, and 78.8% on MOVi-C; with TF2 it is 70.2%, 67.3%, and 68.9%. Thus even a correct factored image representation fails to induce systematic answer composition. Model results near 50–59% on hard splits are only modestly above question-only baselines around 41–48%.

key_findings.claim: Compression baselines show that token count alone does not explain slot performance, but they do not furnish a training-matched non-object-centric control.
key_findings.evidence: Reducing dense features to seven tokens with k-means is very poor; using the paper's multiscale 128-token k-means largely closes the gap in several TF5 settings. A learned seven-query cross-attention reducer still trails slots, and expanding slots with cross-attention rarely helps. However, k-means is untrained and the cross-attention reducer is trained only with VQA, whereas the slot bottleneck receives 300k reconstruction steps, leaving objective and adaptation confounded with object structure.

key_findings.claim: The unseen-background check preserves the main ranking on MOVi-C, but it is a narrow synthetic robustness test rather than evidence of real-world transfer.
key_findings.evidence: With unseen MOVi-C backgrounds, accuracies remain close to the main COOD results and object-centric features retain their larger advantage in hard/small-model settings. No real images, corruptions beyond backgrounds, cross-dataset transfer, or real VQA benchmark is evaluated in the new benchmark.

key_findings.claim: The default seven-slot configuration is not optimal, so object-centric conclusions depend materially on slot-count selection even within this controlled setting.
key_findings.evidence: Seven slots are chosen as maximum objects plus background, but nine or eleven slots often improve CLEVRTex COOD. With TF5 on easy, for example, 11 slots reach 85.7 versus 82.5 for seven; on hard they reach 56.8 versus 55.5. The authors argue this strengthens the OC case because added downstream cost is small, but it also shows that 'one slot per object plus background' is not the operative optimum.

anchors.section: D Choice of number of slots

key_findings.claim: The paper reports a broad grid of point estimates but no run-to-run or split-to-split uncertainty, which is especially consequential for its sub-point hard-setting claims.
key_findings.evidence: The methods and complete appendix specify architectures, learning rates, step budgets, and tables, but no number of random seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or repeated random combination partitions. Approximately 42 questions share each image representation, so 1.7M question–answer pairs do not constitute 1.7M independent visual samples.

anchors.section: C Compute and D Additional Comparisons

method.core_idea: Construct controlled multi-object VQA worlds whose test images use held-out object-property combinations, then compare dense foundation-model patch features with compact Slot Attention reconstructions while sweeping combination diversity, image count, downstream transformer capacity, representation resizing, and downstream training FLOPs.
method.mechanism: CLEVRTex-, Super-CLEVR-, and MOVi-C-style renderers generate easy/medium/hard allowed-combination subsets and a fixed COOD set. DINOv2 or SigLIP2 features feed either directly into a TF2/TF5 VQA transformer or through dataset-pretrained DINOSAURv2/SigLIPSAUR2 slots. K-means and learned cross-attention alter token count; T5-base encodes questions; question-only and ground-truth-object oracles bound performance. Compute-normalized checkpoints and nested sample-size subsets trace accuracy surfaces.
assumptions: Every COOD object is a novel combination of individually seen properties; this is impossible for MOVi-C hard under the stated cardinalities.
Randomly selected combination subsets preserve comparable primitive-property coverage and answer distributions across easy, medium, and hard splits.
Seven Slot Attention vectors are object-aligned and their advantage arises from object structure rather than compression, extra in-domain pretraining, or a reconstruction objective.
Dataset-specific 300k-step slot pretraining can be compared causally with an unadapted dense encoder when the stated target is representation type.
A downstream cross-attention reducer trained only through VQA is a fair control for a separately pretrained Slot Attention bottleneck.
VQA accuracy on generated questions isolates visual compositionality despite language priors, repeated questions per image, and downstream-reasoner failure.
Downstream transformer FLOPs are the relevant compute budget even when feature extraction, resizing, and OC pretraining are excluded.
One reported training trajectory and one random combination partition are representative of model and split variability.
Synthetic renderer diversity and one unseen-background check predict performance in real imagery and natural-language VQA.
The oracle's residual COOD failure does not qualitatively alter comparisons among imperfect visual representations.

techniques.role: Creates nominal easy, medium, and hard training worlds plus fixed held-out object-combination tests.
Produces roughly 42 templated questions per rendered image with dataset-specific answer vocabularies.
Pretrains Slot Attention models to reconstruct DINOv2 or SigLIP2 features for each dataset variant.
Uses two- and five-layer transformer decoders to measure how easily each representation supports answering.
Feeds exact visible object properties to the VQA transformer to expose downstream compositional limits.
Measures answer and question-template priors without image information.
Maps dense features down to slot size or slot features up to dense size with learned queries.
Builds untrained 7- or 128-token summaries of dense patch features as compact controls.
Allocates checkpoint and step budgets according to VQA-transformer FLOPs for each representation size.
Sweeps image count and admissible combination diversity to separate their empirical trends.
Tests MOVi-C COOD images rendered with backgrounds absent from training.
Varies slots and downstream depth/width to audit two important capacity choices.

evaluations.setting: CLEVRTex, Super-CLEVR, and MOVi-C easy/medium/hard worlds with 40k training images, 4k ID images, 4k fixed COOD images, and about 42 questions per image (pp. 3–6; p. 13).
evaluations.metric: ID and COOD VQA accuracy for a question-only model and a ground-truth-object oracle.
evaluations.result: Lower diversity raises ID accuracy but lowers COOD; even the TF5 oracle falls to 67.0–78.8% on hard COOD, showing a substantial downstream reasoning ceiling.
evaluations.baseline: Question-only inputs and exact visible object-property tokens.

evaluations.setting: DINOv2/DINOSAURv2 and SigLIP2/SigLIPSAUR2 across three worlds, three diversity levels, and TF2 versus TF5 decoders (pp. 6–8; pp. 22–24).
evaluations.metric: Absolute COOD VQA accuracy and point delta from the corresponding dense encoder.
evaluations.result: Slots are usually better with TF2, by as much as 12.3 points; with TF5, dense encoders often lead on easy/medium and hard differences are generally between −0.8 and +0.9 points.
evaluations.baseline: Unadapted DINOv2 or SigLIP2 patch-token representations.

evaluations.setting: Seven-token and 128-token k-means summaries plus cross-attention reduction/expansion controls for both backbone families (pp. 5, 7–8, 14, and 24).
evaluations.metric: COOD accuracy at smaller or larger representation sizes.
evaluations.result: Seven-token k-means loses heavily; 128-token k-means can approach dense/slot TF5 results; learned dense-to-seven cross-attention remains below pretrained slots, while expanding slots rarely helps.
evaluations.baseline: Original dense features and original seven-slot representations.

evaluations.setting: Super-CLEVR DINO-family accuracy traced against cumulative downstream-transformer FLOPs under compute-normalized step budgets (pp. 7–8; pp. 16–19).
evaluations.metric: COOD accuracy versus PFLOPs and compute multiplier needed to match the slot model.
evaluations.result: DINOSAURv2 leads at low budgets; DINOv2 needs about 1.5× compute to match easy and does not match hard within 3×, but preprocessing, resizing, and 300k-step slot-pretraining FLOPs are omitted.
evaluations.baseline: Dense, resized-dense, k-means, slot, and resized-slot feature sequences under downstream-only FLOP accounting.

evaluations.setting: Training subsets from 2^10 to 2^15 images plus 40k, crossed with easy/medium/hard diversity and TF2/TF5 (pp. 8–9; pp. 28–29).
evaluations.metric: COOD VQA accuracy as a function of image count and allowed-combination diversity.
evaluations.result: Slots lead broadly at low sample count and with TF2; dense features catch up mainly at the full, diverse dataset with TF5; higher combination diversity often beats simply adding images.
evaluations.baseline: The matching dense encoder and the full-data question-only model.

evaluations.setting: MOVi-C COOD rendered with backgrounds absent from training, for both backbone families and decoder sizes (pp. 19–20).
evaluations.metric: VQA accuracy across easy, medium, and hard combination splits.
evaluations.result: Accuracy remains close to the standard-background COOD result and the same conditional OC ranking persists; no real-image shift is tested.
evaluations.baseline: The corresponding MOVi-C COOD split with training-distribution backgrounds.

evaluations.setting: DINOSAURv2 with 5, 7, 9, or 11 slots on CLEVRTex for TF2 and TF5 (pp. 19–20).
evaluations.metric: COOD VQA accuracy across diversity levels.
evaluations.result: Seven slots outperform five, but nine or eleven are often better; the largest easy TF5 gain is 85.7 versus 82.5, showing sensitivity to slot count.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's default seven slots, chosen as maximum objects plus one background slot.

evaluations.setting: DINOv2 and DINOSAURv2 with deeper or wider downstream transformers on CLEVRTex (pp. 19–20).
evaluations.metric: COOD accuracy for TF5, TF10, TF15, larger feed-forward width, and d_model=256 variants.
evaluations.result: No larger variant consistently beats default TF5 despite greater compute; one wide DINOv2 hard result reaches 56.2 versus 55.4, while most alternatives decline.
evaluations.baseline: Default five-layer, d_model=128, hidden-size-128 downstream transformer.

limitations: Author-stated future scope: the benchmark is synthetic, and effectiveness on real-world imagery remains to be investigated.
Author-stated future scope: more diverse datasets and better architectural choices may change the conclusions.
Reviewer-inferred: MOVi-C hard has fewer allowed combinations than shape categories, contradicting the claim that COOD only recombines individually seen properties.
Reviewer-inferred: random combination selection is not documented as stratified by primitive coverage, object frequency, question type, or answer balance.

Reviewer-inferred: each slot model receives 300k steps of dataset-variant-specific reconstruction pretraining, while dense baselines receive no matched adaptation, so representation structure is not isolated.
Reviewer-inferred: compute efficiency counts only the downstream VQA transformer and explicitly omits cross-attention resizing, feature extraction, and upstream slot pretraining.
Reviewer-inferred: no random-seed count, repeated combination partition, standard deviation, confidence interval, or statistical test is reported.
Reviewer-inferred: roughly 42 questions share each rendered image and image representation, so question-level sample counts substantially overstate independent visual evidence.
Reviewer-inferred: TF5 hard-setting slot/dense differences are mostly below one percentage point and cannot be ranked confidently without uncertainty.
Reviewer-inferred: the ground-truth oracle's large hard-COOD failure shows the downstream reasoning model and split protocol impose a strong ceiling independent of visual representation.
Reviewer-inferred: seven-token k-means is an aggressively lossy untrained control, while 128-token k-means is not representation-size matched; neither is training-matched to slots.
Reviewer-inferred: SigLIPSAUR2 is called object-centric by construction, but the paper does not report masks, segmentation, object-slot purity, or identifiability for this new variant.
Reviewer-inferred: all downstream conclusions use frozen/pretrained feature families and generated VQA templates; end-to-end adaptation, free-form language, and real task transfer are absent.
Reviewer-inferred: the unseen-background test covers one synthetic renderer and one shift type, not textures, occlusion, clutter, camera shift, or real backgrounds.
Reviewer-inferred: the ID–COOD correlations pool related model/configuration points and do not establish that high ID performance causes compositional generalization.
failure_modes: A nominal combination holdout can inadvertently withhold entire primitive categories, turning compositional generalization into ordinary category OOD.
Dataset-adapted slot models may win because of extra target-domain optimization rather than object factorization.
Generated VQA can reward question/answer priors or memorized attribute frequencies even when the visual composition is not understood.
When the downstream reasoner itself fails on ground-truth object lists, better visual features may not translate into systematic answers.
Small single-run gaps can reverse across initialization, data partition, checkpoint choice, slot count, or decoder capacity.
Ignoring upstream and resizing compute can reverse the deployment or training-efficiency ranking.
A fixed seven-slot bottleneck can merge objects, split parts, or allocate extra slots inconsistently when object count and granularity vary.
Synthetic background robustness may not survive real texture, occlusion, segmentation ambiguity, or open-vocabulary questions.
Aggressive token compression can erase fine spatial relations, making a baseline look non-compositional for information-loss reasons.
reusable_insights: Cross sample count with combination diversity: more images and more factor coverage are distinct interventions and can have different breakpoints.
Always include a ground-truth structured oracle; its OOD failure reveals how much of the benchmark is a downstream reasoning problem.
Compare representation formats over an accuracy–compute curve rather than at one decoder size, but state precisely which compute stages are counted.
Audit held-out-combination splits with a coverage matrix proving that every primitive value appears in training at every difficulty.
Use both learned compression and untrained clustering controls, while matching their pretraining data, objectives, token count, and optimization budget.
Report results by question family and by object-property combination, not only aggregate accuracy over many correlated questions per image.
Treat slot count as a tuned capacity parameter rather than assuming one slot per object plus background is optimal.
open_questions: Do the main rankings survive stratified splits that guarantee every primitive property value appears sufficiently often in every training set?
What happens when dense baselines receive the same 300k-step in-domain reconstruction or parameter-efficient adaptation budget as slot models?
What are the results across at least five training seeds and several independent combination partitions with image-clustered confidence intervals?
Does SigLIPSAUR2 actually bind one object per slot, and does slot purity mediate COOD accuracy?
How do conclusions change under end-to-end feature fine-tuning or a stronger symbolic/compositional downstream reasoner?
What is the end-to-end wall-clock, energy, and inference-memory trade-off after counting feature extraction, resizing, and OC pretraining?
Do slot advantages transfer to real multi-object images, open-ended VQA, rare compositions, and natural language questions?
Which question families—counting, attribute query, comparison, spatial relation, or existence—produce the observed advantage?
Can a training-matched low-rank or Perceiver-style dense compressor reproduce the slot benefit without object masks?
How much of the sample-efficiency result is driven by diversity, per-combination frequency, or different answer distributions?

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Object-Centric Representations in Visual Question Answering: Comparative Insights with Foundation Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Mamaghan et al. already compare 15 upstream representations through more than 600 VQA models on synthetic and real data, including object-centric and foundation features. The present paper reuses that downstream setup but contributes controlled held-out property combinations, three richer synthetic worlds, and joint diversity/sample/compute sweeps; it is not the first broad OC-versus-foundation VQA comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Successes and Limitations of Object-centric Models at Compositional Generalisation
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest prior test of object-property composition
competitive_landscape.difference: Montero et al. directly test whether object-centric models reconstruct novel combinations of object properties and analyze both successes and a remaining limitation, but in a simpler single-object/generative setting. The present benchmark moves to multi-object, texture-rich VQA and foundation-feature slots while adding compute and data controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Imagine the Unseen World: A Benchmark for Systematic Generalization in Visual World Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kim et al.'s SVIB already varies the fraction of factor combinations observed during training and evaluates one-step visual-world transformations. The present work adopts the combination-coverage idea for static multi-object VQA and focuses on representation probes rather than generative dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization and Robustness Implications in Object-Centric Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Dittadi et al. evaluate several unsupervised OC models across five datasets under unseen object properties and global corruptions, finding benefits on structured shifts but variable robustness elsewhere. The present paper targets held-out property combinations in VQA and stronger foundation backbones, but covers fewer shift types and no real images.

competitive_landscape.title: Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization?
competitive_landscape.difference: Uselis et al. systematically separate sample scale, concept diversity, and combination coverage, prove a role for linearly factored structure, and test DINO/CLIP. The present work adds explicit slot representations and multi-object VQA, but its diversity conclusion is not new and it does not identify the representation structure theoretically.

competitive_landscape.title: Pretraining Frequency Predicts Compositional Generalization of CLIP on Real-World Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Wiedemer et al. connect CLIP's real-world unseen-combination retrieval to individual-object pretraining frequencies. The present controlled renderer removes unknown web-pretraining overlap and adds slots, but cannot establish that its synthetic ranking transfers to real compositions.

competitive_landscape.title: Deciphering the Role of Representation Disentanglement: Investigating Compositional Generalization in CLIP Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbasi et al. synthesize combinations designed to be absent from CLIP training and relate image/text disentanglement metrics to COOD performance. The present work compares dense and slot features in multi-object VQA but does not measure disentanglement or prove which representation property causes the gap.

competitive_landscape.title: Are We Done with Object-Centric Learning?
competitive_landscape.relationship: alternative object-centric construction and OOD critique
competitive_landscape.difference: Rubinstein et al. show that training-free segmentation-plus-encoding can outperform slot-based OCL on a real OOD task and directly question whether slot separation causes broader generalization. The present paper compares slots with dense/k-means features but omits segmentation-based object encoders and real OOD evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Zero-Shot Object-Centric Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Didolkar et al. introduce the DINOv2-based object-centric approach and benchmark zero-shot object discovery across eight synthetic and real datasets. The present paper uses DINOSAURv2 and extends the recipe to SigLIP2, but trains a separate slot model per dataset variant and evaluates VQA rather than zero-shot object discovery.

competitive_landscape.title: Provably Learning Object-Centric Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Brady et al. give compositionality and irreducibility conditions under which ground-truth object representations are identifiable and link those properties to empirical models. The present study supplies broader downstream evidence but neither verifies its slots satisfy those conditions nor connects identifiability to its VQA gains.

competitive_landscape.title: An Investigation into Pre-Training Object-Centric Representations for Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Yoon et al. systematically test OC pretraining for RL, including sample efficiency, OOD generalization, visual complexity, and pooling choices, and report both benefits and limitations. The present work targets property-compositional VQA with foundation features and more explicit combination controls.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first fair, systematic multi-world VQA comparison showing that object-centric representations yield stronger compositional generalization whenever training diversity, sample size, or downstream compute is constrained, and introduces SigLIPSAUR2 plus a controlled benchmark.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The empirical contribution is a substantial grid over three texture-rich synthetic worlds, two foundation families and their slot variants, two downstream capacities, representation resizing and clustering controls, combination diversity, sample count, downstream FLOPs, OOD backgrounds, slot count, and decoder capacity. However, same-team work already performs extensive OC-versus-foundation VQA, Montero et al. already test object-property composition, Kim et al. already vary combination coverage, and Uselis et al. already separate diversity from scale.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is the integration of these axes into a reusable multi-object VQA benchmark and the extension of foundation-feature slots to SigLIP2, not the first evidence that OC helps VQA or property composition. The headline causal interpretation is weakened because slots alone receive 300k steps of dataset-specific pretraining, compute omits that phase, hard MOVi-C cannot contain every primitive in training, and no uncertainty accompanies many sub-point comparisons. Results support a conditional empirical advantage for this trained compact bottleneck under downstream constraints; they do not isolate object binding as the cause or establish real-world superiority.

reviewer_notes: All 29 extracted pages of arXiv v1 were read, including the full result tables, data attributes, hyperparameters, FLOP accounting, sample-size figures, and Appendices A–D; main tables and Figures 2–5 were directly inspected in the PDF. The MOVi-C hard-split contradiction follows directly from the paper's stated 36×3 object space and 20% training cardinality. Eleven primary competitor records were checked against official arXiv submission histories on 2026-08-23. No seeds or uncertainty were found anywhere in the full text. This is a primary full-text review, not independent secondary verification.
